strand.title: Algebra
strand.metaDescription: GCSE algebra: notation, vocabulary and manipulation, graphs, solving equations and inequalities, sequences.

topics.title: Notation, vocabulary and manipulation
topics.cardDescription: Notation, substitution, simplifying, factorising, formulae and proof.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE algebraic notation, vocabulary and manipulation: simplifying, expanding, factorising, changing the subject, algebraic fractions, functions and proof.

subtopics.title: Algebraic notation
subtopics.description: Writing products and quotients without symbols, so 3 × y is 3y.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover ab for a × b, 3y for 3 × y and y + y + y, a/b for a ÷ b, brackets, and coefficients written as fractions rather than decimals. Products and quotients only: powers like a² sit on the squares-and-cubes page, and index laws in the simplifying group. Both tiers. (A1)

subtopics.title: Squares and cubes of a letter
subtopics.description: What a², a³ and 2a each mean, and why a² and 2a are not the same thing.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover a² as a × a, a³ as a × a × a and a²b as a × a × b, contrasting a² with 2a and a³ with 3a, with small numeric checks. Out of scope: index laws (simplifying group); negative and fractional indices belong to the Number strand, fractional ones Higher there. Both tiers. (A1)

subtopics.title: Terms, factors and coefficients
subtopics.description: Naming terms, factors and coefficients in an expression.
subtopics.coverNote: Name the terms of an expression, the factors within a term, and coefficients, including negative, fractional and the implied 1 or −1, plus constant terms. Out of scope: factorising (factorising group) and classifying whole statements as expression, equation or formula (sibling page). Both tiers. (A3)

subtopics.title: Expression, equation or formula
subtopics.description: Deciding which a piece of algebra is from its equals sign and its letters.
subtopics.coverNote: Classify a given piece of algebra as expression, equation, formula, identity or inequality, using the presence of an equals or inequality sign and whether letters are unknowns to find or quantities linked by a rule. The identity sign ≡ is only met here; full treatment sits on the equation-or-identity page. Both tiers. (A3)

subtopics.title: Writing an expression from words
subtopics.description: Turning descriptions of ages, costs or lengths into expressions.
subtopics.coverNote: Translate worded descriptions of ages, costs, lengths and think-of-a-number chains into expressions, inserting brackets where order requires, e.g. 3(x + 2) versus 3x + 2. Expressions only: building whole formulae is the writing-a-formula page, and forming then solving equations lives on the equations topic. Both tiers. (A21)

subtopics.title: Substituting into an expression
subtopics.description: Replacing each letter with a number, then evaluating in the right order.
subtopics.coverNote: Substitute positive integers, simple decimals and fractions into expressions in one or two letters, applying the order of operations, e.g. 3a + 2b or 5(x − 2). Boundaries: negative inputs and squared terms have their own sibling pages; formulae in context sit on substituting-into-formulae. Both tiers. (A2)

subtopics.title: Substituting negative numbers
subtopics.description: Substituting a negative value with brackets, so the sign survives squaring.
subtopics.coverNote: Substitute negative values wrapped in brackets, covering (−3)² versus −3², subtracting a negative, and products of two negatives, in expressions like 2x² − 3x with x = −4. Boundaries: positive-only substitution and formula work sit on the sibling pages; the sign conventions themselves are Number-strand material. Both tiers. (A2)

subtopics.title: Substituting into terms with powers
subtopics.description: Why 3x² means square first then multiply by 3, so x = 4 gives 48 not 144.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover why 3x² squares first then multiplies by 3, so x = 4 gives 48 not 144, contrasting (3x)²; include cubes and mixed expressions like 2x² + x, and simple fractional inputs. Out of scope: index laws (simplifying group) and negative inputs (sibling page). Both tiers. (A2)

subtopics.title: Substituting into a formula
subtopics.description: Using formulae such as v = u + at by substituting every known value.
subtopics.coverNote: Substitute several known values into standard and scientific formulae, e.g. v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², F = ma, reading units from context. The DfE formulae appendix lists the kinematics formulae as provided in examinations, not memorised. Rearranging first belongs on changing-the-subject. Both tiers. (A2, A5)

subtopics.title: Collecting like terms
subtopics.description: Combining like terms, each term carrying the sign in front of it.
subtopics.coverNote: Simplify by combining like terms in one or two letters plus constants, each term keeping the sign in front of it, e.g. 5a + 3b − 2a + b; treat 3ab and 2ba as like terms. Powers (x versus x²) are the sibling page; multiplying terms is a separate page. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: Like terms with powers
subtopics.description: Why x and x² are unlike terms, and collecting expressions that mix them.
subtopics.coverNote: Establish x, x² and x³ as unlike terms, then collect expressions mixing them, e.g. 4x² + 3x − x² + 5x, plus pairs like xy versus x. Out of scope: adding indices when multiplying, which is the multiplying-powers page, not collecting. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: Multiplying terms
subtopics.description: Multiplying coefficients and letters separately, so 3a × 4b is 12ab.
subtopics.coverNote: Multiply coefficients and letters separately: 3a × 4b = 12ab, a × a = a², 2a × 5a = 10a², including negative coefficients and three-factor products. Higher powers via index laws, like 4a³ × 3a², sit on multiplying-powers; brackets sit in the expanding group. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: Dividing terms
subtopics.description: Writing a division as a fraction, then cancelling common factors.
subtopics.coverNote: Write divisions as fractions and cancel common numeric and letter factors, e.g. 12ab ÷ 3a = 4b, including quotients that leave a fractional coefficient. Boundaries: subtracting indices, like 12a⁵ ÷ 4a², is the dividing-powers page; fractions with polynomial numerators are the Higher algebraic-fractions pages. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: Multiplying powers of a letter
subtopics.description: Simplifying 4a³ × 3a² by multiplying coefficients and adding indices.
subtopics.coverNote: Apply aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ to terms with coefficients, e.g. 4a³ × 3a² = 12a⁵, including two letters like 2a²b × 3ab³. Positive integer indices only; negative and fractional indices are Number-strand work, the fractional ones Higher there. Both tiers — the laws are applied here, derived on Number. (A4)

subtopics.title: Dividing powers of a letter
subtopics.description: Simplifying 12a⁵ ÷ 4a² by dividing coefficients and subtracting indices.
subtopics.coverNote: Apply aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ with coefficients, e.g. 12a⁵ ÷ 4a² = 3a³, written as fractions where helpful, including two-letter quotients. Keep the larger index on top so results stay positive; zero and negative indices belong to the Number strand. Both tiers per A4. (A4)

subtopics.title: Raising a term to a power
subtopics.description: Applying the index to every factor, so (2a³)⁴ is 16a¹² not 2a¹².
subtopics.coverNote: Raise a whole term to a power, applying the index to every factor: (2a³)⁴ = 16a¹², (ab²)³ = a³b⁶, contrasting with the error 2a¹²; include squaring and cubing simple terms and negative coefficients to even and odd powers. Fractional indices are Higher Number work. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: Expanding a single bracket
subtopics.description: Multiplying the outside term over every term inside, not just the first.
subtopics.coverNote: Multiply a positive term over a bracket: number outside, letter outside giving x², and mixed terms, e.g. 3(x + 2), x(x − 4), 2a(3a + b), reaching every term inside. A negative term outside is the sibling page; pairs of brackets come later in the group. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: A minus sign in front of a bracket
subtopics.description: Expanding with a negative term outside, where the second sign inside flips.
subtopics.coverNote: Expand with a negative term outside, e.g. −(x − 3), −2(3x + 5) and 7 − 2(x − 4), where the second sign inside flips; name the classic error of leaving that last sign unchanged. Combining two expanded brackets is the expand-and-collect page. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: Expanding then collecting like terms
subtopics.description: Simplifying 3(x + 2) − 2(x − 5), the minus acting on the whole second bracket.
subtopics.coverNote: Expand two single brackets and collect like terms, e.g. 3(x + 2) − 2(x − 5), the subtraction acting on the whole second bracket; include addition cases and letter terms outside. Out of scope: products of two brackets, which is expanding-double-brackets. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: Expanding double brackets
subtopics.description: Multiplying every term in one bracket by every term in the other.
subtopics.coverNote: Expand (x + a)(x + b) in all four sign combinations by grid or FOIL, collecting the two middle terms. Coefficients of x stay 1 here: (2x + 3)(3x − 1) is the sibling page, squaring a bracket its own page, and three brackets the Higher page. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: Double brackets with coefficients
subtopics.description: Expanding (2x + 3)(3x − 1), keeping track of the middle terms.
subtopics.coverNote: Expand products like (2x + 3)(3x − 1) and (5 − 2x)(x + 4), tracking coefficient products in the middle terms; include two-variable cases like (2x + y)(x − 3y). Both tiers — A4 leaves products of two binomials unbraced, so Foundation meets these too. Triple products are Higher. (A4)

subtopics.title: Squaring a bracket
subtopics.description: Writing (x + 4)² as a full double bracket, never just x² + 16.
subtopics.coverNote: Write (x + 4)² as (x + 4)(x + 4) and expand fully, killing the x² + 16 error; include (x − a)² and coefficient cases like (2x + 3)². State the pattern a² + 2ab + b² as a check rather than a shortcut. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: Expanding triple brackets
subtopics.description: Multiplying two brackets first, then the third into the result.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, per the A4 braces on products of more than two binomials. Multiply two brackets, then the third into the quadratic result, keeping every term; include a repeated bracket like (x + 2)²(x − 1). Out of scope: binomial expansion of (a + b)ⁿ, which is A level. (A4)

subtopics.title: Taking out a common factor
subtopics.description: Factorising into a single bracket by taking out the highest common factor.
subtopics.coverNote: Factorise into a single bracket by extracting a common numeric or single-letter factor, e.g. 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3), x² + 5x = x(x + 5), checking by expanding back. The complete highest common factor, numbers and letters together, is the sibling page. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: Factorising completely
subtopics.description: Taking out the whole common factor, numbers and letters together.
subtopics.coverNote: Extract the full highest common factor, coefficients and letters together, e.g. 6x²y + 9xy² = 3xy(2x + 3y), so nothing shared remains inside the bracket; include three-term examples and contrast with partly factorised answers. Two-bracket quadratic factorising starts on the next page. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: Factorising a quadratic expression
subtopics.description: Factorising x² + bx + c from a pair of numbers that add to b and multiply to c.
subtopics.coverNote: Factorise x² + bx + c into two brackets from a pair summing to b and multiplying to c, covering all sign cases: c positive with b negative, c negative, and b zero pointing to the difference-of-squares page. Coefficient a > 1 is the Higher sibling; solving the equations is the equations topic. Both tiers. (A4)

subtopics.title: The difference of two squares
subtopics.description: Factorising expressions like x² − 49, spotted by the two squares and the minus.
subtopics.coverNote: Factorise a² − b² forms spotted from two squares and a minus. Foundation: x² − 49 and other x² − a² shapes. Higher: coefficient and two-variable forms like 4x² − 9 and 25x² − y², which fall under the A4 braces for ax² + bx + c. State that a sum of squares does not factorise. (A4)

subtopics.title: Factorising when x² has a coefficient
subtopics.description: Factorising ax² + bx + c by splitting the middle term or testing brackets.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, per the A4 braces. Factorise ax² + bx + c by splitting the middle term or testing bracket pairs, with negative b and c included; always extract any common factor first, and check by expanding. Solving these equations, with the formula and completing the square, is the equations topic. (A4)

subtopics.title: Writing a formula from a description
subtopics.description: Building a formula from a worded rule, such as a charge with a fixed part.
subtopics.coverNote: Build a formula from a rule in words, e.g. cost as fixed charge plus rate, pay from hours, perimeter rules; define each letter and put the subject on the left. Out of scope: rearranging (sibling pages), substituting values (substitution group), and deriving equations to solve (equations topic). Both tiers. (A21, A5)

subtopics.title: Changing the subject of a formula
subtopics.description: Rearranging a formula so a different letter stands alone on one side.
subtopics.coverNote: Rearrange formulae by inverse operations where the subject appears once and unpowered, e.g. v = u + at for t, y = mx + c for x, including subjects inside a bracket or multiplied by a fraction. Squares, roots and twice-appearing subjects are the sibling pages, the latter Higher. Both tiers. (A5)

subtopics.title: Rearranging with squares and roots
subtopics.description: Changing the subject when it sits inside a square, a root or a fraction.
subtopics.coverNote: Change the subject when it sits inside a square, square root or denominator, e.g. v² = u² + 2as for u, undoing the outermost layer first; take the positive root unless context demands otherwise. The subject appearing twice is the Higher sibling; substituting values is the substitution group. Both tiers. (A5)

subtopics.title: The subject appearing twice
subtopics.description: Gathering both copies of the subject on one side, then factorising it out.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page. Gather both copies of the subject on one side, factorise it out, then divide, e.g. make x the subject of ax + b = cx + d or y = (x + 1)/(x − 2), clearing the fraction first. Single-appearance rearrangement, including powers and roots, belongs to the sibling pages. (A5)

subtopics.title: Simplifying an algebraic fraction
subtopics.description: Factorising before cancelling, since only a factor cancels, never a term.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, per the A4 braces on algebraic fractions. Factorise numerator and denominator before cancelling, with common factors up to quadratics, e.g. (x² − 9)/(x² + 5x + 6); name the crime of cancelling terms across a plus sign. Adding, multiplying and dividing are the sibling pages. (A4)

subtopics.title: Multiplying and dividing algebraic fractions
subtopics.description: Cancelling before multiplying, and dividing as multiplying by the reciprocal.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page under the A4 braces. Multiply numerators and denominators after factorising and cancelling; divide by multiplying by the reciprocal. Include quadratic factorising inside the fractions and linear-with-quadratic mixes. Solving equations containing algebraic fractions belongs to the equations topic under A18 rearrangement. (A4)

subtopics.title: Adding and subtracting algebraic fractions
subtopics.description: Writing both fractions over a common denominator before adding or subtracting.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page under the A4 braces. Add and subtract over a common denominator, with numeric, linear and paired-bracket denominators like (x + 1)(x − 2); expand carefully when subtracting the second numerator. Leave answers as one simplified fraction; equations built from them are solved on the equations topic. (A4)

subtopics.title: Functions as inputs and outputs
subtopics.description: An expression as a machine turning inputs into outputs, run both ways.
subtopics.coverNote: Interpret expressions as function machines with inputs and outputs, run forwards and, by inverse operations, backwards; cover two-step machines, tables of inputs against outputs, and finding the input for a given output. Formal f(x) notation, inverses and composites are the Higher sibling pages. Both tiers. (A7)

subtopics.title: Function notation
subtopics.description: Reading f(x) as the output at x, and evaluating f(3) and 2f(1).
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page. Read f(x) as the output at x; evaluate f(3), f(−2), 2f(1) and f(a) as an expression; solve f(x) = k for linear and quadratic rules. Out of scope: domain and range language, which is A level; inverse and composite functions are the sibling pages. (A7)

subtopics.title: Inverse functions
subtopics.description: Finding f⁻¹(x) by rearranging y = f(x), and how the inverse undoes it.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A7 braces. Find f⁻¹(x) by writing y = f(x), rearranging for x and swapping letters, for linear rules and simple fractions like f(x) = (x + 2)/3; interpret the inverse as undoing, so f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. Domain restrictions and reflection in y = x are A level. (A7)

subtopics.title: Composite functions
subtopics.description: Applying one function to the output of another, and why fg(x) applies g first.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A7 braces. Form fg(x) and gf(x), applying the inner function first; evaluate numerically, e.g. fg(2), and as simplified expressions, including ff(x). Contrast fg with gf to show order matters. Inverses of composites and domain questions are A level. (A7)

subtopics.title: Telling an equation from an identity
subtopics.description: An equation holds for some values, an identity for all, written with ≡.
subtopics.coverNote: Distinguish an equation, true for particular values, from an identity, true for all values and recorded with ≡; verify identities by expanding, refute false ones with a single counterexample value, and sort formula and inequality into the same vocabulary. Step-by-step equivalence arguments are the sibling page. Both tiers. (A3, A6)

subtopics.title: Showing two expressions are equivalent
subtopics.description: Expanding and simplifying one side until it matches the other.
subtopics.coverNote: Show two expressions are equivalent by expanding and simplifying one side until it matches the other, e.g. (x + 3)² − 9 ≡ x² + 6x, giving a reason per step and working from one side only. Both tiers. Integer representation tools and full proofs are the Higher siblings. (A6)

subtopics.title: Writing even, odd and consecutive integers
subtopics.description: Even numbers as 2n, odd as 2n + 1, consecutive integers as n and n + 1.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page feeding algebraic proof. Represent an even number as 2n, an odd as 2n + 1, consecutive integers as n and n + 1, consecutive evens as 2n and 2n + 2, and multiples of k as kn, stating that n is an integer every time. Complete proofs sit on the sibling page. (A6)

subtopics.title: Proving a statement algebraically
subtopics.description: Proving a claim for every integer at once, since examples never prove.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A6 braces on proofs. Prove parity, divisibility and consecutive-integer statements algebraically, e.g. the difference of consecutive squares is odd; stress that substituted examples demonstrate but never prove, and that one counterexample disproves. Proof by induction or contradiction is A level. (A6)

topics.title: Graphs
topics.cardDescription: Straight lines, curves, transformations, real-life graphs and the circle.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE graphs: coordinates, straight lines, quadratic and other curves, graph transformations, real-life graphs, gradients, areas and the equation of a circle.

subtopics.title: Coordinates in all four quadrants
subtopics.description: Plotting and reading points with negative coordinates, x written before y.
subtopics.coverNote: Plot and read points across all four quadrants, x written before y, including negative and simple decimal coordinates, points on the axes, and reading from grids in context. Out of scope: midpoints and shape completion, which are the sibling pages; 3D coordinates are beyond GCSE. Both tiers. (A8)

subtopics.title: The midpoint of a line segment
subtopics.description: Finding the point halfway between two points by averaging the coordinates.
subtopics.coverNote: Find the midpoint by averaging x and y coordinates separately, with negative and decimal values, and work backwards from a midpoint and one end to the other end. 2D only. Dividing a segment in a given ratio belongs to the Ratio strand; distance between points sits with Pythagoras on Geometry. Both tiers. (A8)

subtopics.title: Completing a shape from its coordinates
subtopics.description: Finding the missing vertex of a square, rectangle or parallelogram.
subtopics.coverNote: Find the missing vertex of a square, rectangle, parallelogram or right-angled triangle by copying equal sides as horizontal-and-vertical shifts across the grid, including cases with more than one possible answer to list. Formal column-vector notation belongs to the Geometry strand. Both tiers. (A8)

subtopics.title: Horizontal and vertical lines
subtopics.description: Why x = 3 is a vertical line and y = 3 a horizontal one.
subtopics.coverNote: Recognise, draw and name the lines x = a and y = b, including the axes as x = 0 and y = 0, correcting the reflex that x = 3 should be horizontal; identify such lines as mirror lines for later transformation work. Sloping lines start on the following pages. Both tiers. (A9)

subtopics.title: Plotting a line from a table of values
subtopics.description: Filling a table, plotting the points, and using a stray point as a check.
subtopics.coverNote: Complete a table of values from a linear equation including negative x, plot the points, draw the ruled line, and treat a point off the line as an arithmetic alarm; include equations like y = 2x − 3 and y = ½x + 1. Gradients and intercepts are read on the following pages. Both tiers. (A9)

subtopics.title: The gradient of a line
subtopics.description: Measuring steepness as rise over run, the sign showing climb or fall.
subtopics.coverNote: Measure gradient as rise over run from a grid triangle and from two coordinates, with negative gradients for falling lines and fractional gradients included; steeper means larger magnitude. Out of scope: gradients of curves, which are Higher on gradients-and-areas, and writing equations, on the next pages. Both tiers. (A10)

subtopics.title: The equation y = mx + c
subtopics.description: Reading the gradient and y-intercept straight from the equation.
subtopics.coverNote: Read m and c straight from y = mx + c, including negative and fractional m and c = 0, and sketch a line from them; interpret m as steepness and c as the crossing height. Equations not yet in this form are the rearranging sibling page. Both tiers. (A9, A10)

subtopics.title: Reading an equation off a graph
subtopics.description: Finding the intercept on the y-axis and the gradient from a whole-square triangle.
subtopics.coverNote: Find a drawn line's equation: intercept from the y-axis crossing, gradient from a whole-square triangle, then write y = mx + c; include negative and fractional gradients and scales where one square is not one unit. Lines given as coordinate pairs without a picture sit on line-through-two-points. Both tiers. (A9, A10)

subtopics.title: Lines not written as y = mx + c
subtopics.description: Rearranging equations like 2x + 3y = 6 before reading the gradient off.
subtopics.coverNote: Rearrange forms like 2x + 3y = 6 and x + y = 4 into y = mx + c before reading gradient and intercept, and decide whether pairs of such lines are parallel; name the trap of quoting the unrearranged x coefficient as the gradient. Both tiers. (A9, A10)

subtopics.title: The line through a point with a given gradient
subtopics.description: Substituting the point into y = mx + c to find c, then writing the equation out.
subtopics.coverNote: Find the equation of the line with a given gradient through a given point by substituting the point into y = mx + c to find c; include negative and fractional gradients and points with negative coordinates. The two-point version is the sibling; perpendicular gradients are Higher. Both tiers. (A9)

subtopics.title: The line through two points
subtopics.description: Finding the gradient from the two points, then the intercept from either.
subtopics.coverNote: Find the equation of the line through two given points: gradient from the coordinate differences first, then c from either point, checking with the unused one; include negative and fractional answers. Midpoints of the same segment belong to the coordinates group. Both tiers. (A9)

subtopics.title: Parallel lines
subtopics.description: Lines with equal gradients never meet, and writing a parallel line’s equation.
subtopics.coverNote: Identify parallel lines from equal gradients in y = mx + c, including after rearranging, and write the equation of the line parallel to a given one through a given point. Both tiers — the A9 braces cover only perpendicularity, which is the Higher sibling page. (A9)

subtopics.title: Perpendicular lines
subtopics.description: Gradients of perpendicular lines multiply to −1.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A9 braces. Use m₁m₂ = −1: find negative reciprocals, test pairs of equations for perpendicularity, and write the perpendicular line through a given point, including the perpendicular bisector of a segment. Applied to circle tangents on the circles group. (A9)

subtopics.title: Plotting a quadratic graph
subtopics.description: Building a table of values, then drawing a smooth curve through the points.
subtopics.coverNote: Plot quadratics from a table of values including negative x, where squaring the negative is the error to name; draw a smooth freehand curve, no ruled segments or flat bottom. Include y = x² ± c and full x² + bx + c forms. Reading features off the curve is the sibling pages' work. Both tiers. (A12)

subtopics.title: The shape and symmetry of a parabola
subtopics.description: Why a quadratic graph is a symmetric curve with one turning point.
subtopics.coverNote: Establish the parabola's mirror symmetry and single turning point, the sign of the x² coefficient deciding whether it opens upwards or downwards; identify the line of symmetry from a drawn graph. Locating the turning point exactly by completing the square is the Higher sibling. Both tiers. (A11, A12)

subtopics.title: Roots and intercepts on a quadratic graph
subtopics.description: Reading roots off the x-axis and the intercept off the y-axis.
subtopics.coverNote: Read roots where the curve crosses the x-axis and the y-intercept where it crosses the y-axis, from drawn graphs, including two-root, repeated-root and no-root cases. Graphical reading only — deducing roots algebraically by factorising belongs to the equations topic. Both tiers. (A11)

subtopics.title: Turning points on a quadratic graph
subtopics.description: Reading the minimum or maximum off the graph, halfway between the roots.
subtopics.coverNote: Read the minimum or maximum point from a drawn quadratic graph, using symmetry to place it halfway between the roots, and interpret it in context as a greatest or least value. Both tiers for graphical reading — finding it algebraically by completing the square is the Higher sibling. (A11)

subtopics.title: Sketching a quadratic from factorised form
subtopics.description: Marking roots from the brackets and the intercept from the constant.
subtopics.coverNote: Sketch a quadratic from factorised form: roots from the brackets, y-intercept from the constant of the expanded form, correct orientation, smooth labelled curve; include repeated roots. Monic cases only at Foundation. Marking the turning point's coordinates needs the Higher completing-the-square sibling. Both tiers. (A11, A12)

subtopics.title: The turning point by completing the square
subtopics.description: Reading the turning point (−p, q) from (x + p)² + q, signs included.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A11 braces. Read the turning point (−p, q) from (x + p)² + q with signs handled, state minimum or maximum values and the line of symmetry, and sketch with the vertex placed. The completing-the-square technique itself is taught on the equations topic. (A11)

subtopics.title: Cubic graphs
subtopics.description: The S-shaped curve of x³, and how a negative coefficient flips it.
subtopics.coverNote: Plot and recognise simple cubics like y = x³ and y = x³ + 2 from tables of values, cubing negatives correctly; know the S-shape and how a negative coefficient flips it. Out of scope: sketching factorised cubics from roots and turning points, which is A level. Both tiers. (A12)

subtopics.title: Reciprocal graphs
subtopics.description: The two branches of y = 1/x, approaching but never touching either axis.
subtopics.coverNote: Plot and recognise y = 1/x with x ≠ 0: two branches in opposite quadrants approaching but never touching the axes, the word asymptote used informally. A12 names only y = 1/x; general k/x curves arise with inverse proportion on the Ratio strand, and formal asymptote work is A level. Both tiers. (A12)

subtopics.title: Matching an equation to its graph
subtopics.description: Telling linear, quadratic, cubic and reciprocal graphs apart by shape alone.
subtopics.coverNote: Match equations to graph shapes on sight: linear, quadratic, cubic and reciprocal at Foundation; Higher adds exponential, sine, cosine and tangent from the sibling pages. Justify choices by shape, intercepts and end behaviour before plotting anything. Sketching each family belongs on its own page. (A12)

subtopics.title: Exponential graphs
subtopics.description: The shape of y = kˣ, growing or decaying, always crossing the y-axis at 1.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A12 braces. Plot and recognise y = kˣ for positive k: always positive, y-intercept 1, growth for k > 1, decay for k between 0 and 1; read values off and link to repeated percentage change on the Ratio strand. Logarithms and solving kˣ = c exactly are A level. (A12)

subtopics.title: The sine and cosine graphs
subtopics.description: The two waves between −1 and 1, repeating every 360°, separated by a shift.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A12 braces. Sketch y = sin x and y = cos x in degrees for angles of any size, bounded by ±1 with period 360°, cosine as sine shifted 90°; use the symmetry to read further solutions of sin x = k. Radians and amplitude changes are A level. (A12)

subtopics.title: The tangent graph
subtopics.description: The repeating branches of y = tan x, with vertical asymptotes every 180°.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A12 braces. Sketch y = tan x in degrees: period 180°, through the origin, vertical asymptotes at 90° plus multiples of 180° where it is undefined, values unbounded; read solutions across branches. Radians, and any transformation beyond translation and reflection, are A level. (A12)

subtopics.title: Translating a graph up and down
subtopics.description: The graph of f(x) + a as the original slid a units vertically.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A13 braces. Sketch y = f(x) + a as the graph slid a units vertically, on given curves including quadratics and trig graphs; track named points and give the image of a marked point. Horizontal slides and reflections are siblings; stretches like af(x) are A level. (A13)

subtopics.title: Translating a graph left and right
subtopics.description: The graph of f(x + a) as a slide of a units, opposite to the sign.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A13 braces. Sketch y = f(x + a) as a horizontal slide of a units opposite to the sign, on quadratics and trig graphs; track turning points and intercepts and name the wrong-direction trap. Stretches f(ax) are A level; combining with the vertical slide is fair. (A13)

subtopics.title: Reflecting a graph in the axes
subtopics.description: Telling −f(x), a reflection in the x-axis, from f(−x) in the y-axis.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A13 braces. Distinguish y = −f(x), reflection in the x-axis, from y = f(−x), reflection in the y-axis, on quadratics, cubics and trig graphs; give images of marked points. Combining a reflection with a translation is fair; stretches are A level. (A13)

subtopics.title: Distance–time graphs
subtopics.description: Speed as the gradient, rest as a flat section, not a picture of the road.
subtopics.coverNote: Read speed as gradient and rest as horizontal sections on journey graphs including the return leg; calculate speeds with mixed units, find average speed for a whole journey, and correct the graph-as-picture-of-the-road misconception. Curved graphs and tangent gradients are the Higher gradients-and-areas group. Both tiers. (A14)

subtopics.title: Velocity–time graphs
subtopics.description: Acceleration as the gradient and distance as the area underneath.
subtopics.coverNote: Interpret velocity-time graphs against distance-time ones: gradient is acceleration, area beneath is distance. Foundation reads and compares the motion and simple gradients; calculating gradients and areas as acceleration and distance quantitatively is Higher under the A15 braces, taught on the gradients-and-areas group. (A14, A15)

subtopics.title: Reading a financial graph
subtopics.description: Fixed charges as the intercept and the rate as the gradient.
subtopics.coverNote: Read the fixed charge as intercept and the rate as gradient on tariff, wage and unit-conversion graphs; compare two tariffs and interpret the crossing point as break-even. Gradient and area interpretation on curved financial graphs falls under the Higher A15 braces on gradients-and-areas. Both tiers. (A14)

subtopics.title: Estimating values from a real-life graph
subtopics.description: Reading between plotted points for an estimate, and how far to trust it.
subtopics.coverNote: Estimate values by reading between and beyond plotted points on real-context and non-standard graphs, including reciprocal shapes and, at Higher, exponential ones; weigh interpolation against extrapolation and the accuracy the scale allows. Journey and money graphs have their own sibling pages. Both tiers. (A14)

subtopics.title: The gradient of a curve at a point
subtopics.description: Drawing a tangent and taking its gradient, since a curve’s gradient varies.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A15 braces. Draw a tangent to a curve at a point by eye and take its gradient as an estimate, noting a curve's gradient differs at every point and answers vary with the tangent drawn. Differentiation is A level. Interpretation in context sits on the in-context sibling. (A15)

subtopics.title: Average and instantaneous rates of change
subtopics.description: The chord for the average rate, and the tangent for the rate at an instant.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A15 braces. Distinguish the average rate of change, a chord's gradient over an interval, from the instantaneous rate, the tangent's gradient at a point; compute both from drawn graphs in kinematic and container-filling contexts. Calculus notation and exact derivatives are A level. (A15)

subtopics.title: Estimating the area under a graph
subtopics.description: Splitting the region into strips and trapeziums to estimate the area.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A15 braces. Estimate the area under a curve by splitting it into strips of trapeziums, triangles and rectangles, and judge over- or underestimate from whether chords sit above or below the curve. Exact areas by integration are A level; meaning in context is the sibling page. (A15)

subtopics.title: Gradients and areas in context
subtopics.description: On a velocity–time graph the gradient is acceleration and the area distance.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A15 braces. Interpret gradients and areas with units: on velocity-time graphs the gradient is acceleration in m/s² and the area is distance in metres; include distance-time and financial contexts. Combines the tangent, chord and trapezium techniques of the three sibling pages. (A15)

subtopics.title: The equation of a circle
subtopics.description: Why x² + y² = r² describes a circle centred at the origin.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A16 braces. Recognise and use x² + y² = r² for a circle centred at the origin: state the radius from the equation and vice versa, test whether points lie on, inside or outside, and sketch. Circles centred elsewhere, (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r², are A level. (A16)

subtopics.title: The tangent to a circle at a point
subtopics.description: Finding the tangent’s equation from the radius it is perpendicular to.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A16 braces. Find the tangent to x² + y² = r² at a given point: gradient of the radius to the point, negative reciprocal for the tangent, then the equation through the point. Depends on the perpendicular-lines page. Tangents from an external point are A level. (A16)

subtopics.title: Where a line crosses a circle
subtopics.description: Substituting the line into the circle’s equation to count the meeting points.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page. Substitute a linear equation into x² + y² = r² and solve the resulting quadratic, pairing each x with its own y; the number of solutions counts the meeting points, tangency giving a repeated root. Formal discriminant language is A level. Sits under the A19 linear/quadratic braces beside A16. (A16, A19)

groups.lead: Cubic and reciprocal curves, and exponential and trigonometric ones at Higher.

groups.lead: Graphs of journeys, charges and readings, and what gradient and area mean.

groups.lead: Higher tier: how adding moves a graph and a minus sign reflects it.

groups.lead: Higher tier: gradients of curves, rates of change, and areas under graphs.

groups.title: Circles on coordinate axes
groups.lead: Higher tier: the circle x² + y² = r², its tangents, and lines that cross it.

topics.title: Solving equations and inequalities
topics.cardDescription: Linear, quadratic and simultaneous equations, inequalities and iteration.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE solving equations and inequalities: linear, quadratic and simultaneous equations, graphical and iterative methods, and inequalities on number lines and graphs.

subtopics.title: Solving two-step equations
subtopics.description: Undoing operations in reverse order, keeping both sides balanced.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve equations like 3x + 5 = 17 and x/4 − 2 = 1 by undoing operations in reverse order, keeping the balance; include negative and fractional solutions and forms like 10 − 2x = 4. Brackets, fractions around expressions, and unknowns on both sides are the sibling pages. Both tiers. (A17)

subtopics.title: Unknowns on both sides
subtopics.description: Collecting the unknowns on one side and the numbers on the other.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve equations with the unknown on both sides, e.g. 5x − 3 = 2x + 9, collecting unknowns onto the side that keeps the coefficient positive; include traps like 12 − x = 3x + 2 and non-integer answers. Expanding brackets first belongs with the sibling page. Both tiers. (A17)

subtopics.title: Equations with brackets
subtopics.description: Expanding the brackets first, or dividing both sides straight away.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve equations with brackets, e.g. 3(x − 2) = 15, by expanding first or by dividing both sides when the right-hand side divides cleanly; include brackets on both sides like 2(x + 1) = 3(x − 4). Sign slips over a subtracted bracket link back to the notation topic. Both tiers. (A17)

subtopics.title: Equations with fractions
subtopics.description: Clearing fractions by multiplying every term by the common denominator.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve equations with numeric denominators, e.g. x/3 + 2 = 5, (x + 2)/3 = 4 and (2x − 1)/3 = (x + 2)/4, multiplying every term by the common denominator, whole-number terms included. Unknowns in the denominator lead to quadratics and are Higher via A18 rearrangement. Both tiers. (A17)

subtopics.title: Solving a quadratic by factorising
subtopics.description: Factorising, then setting each bracket to zero, since a factor must be zero.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve quadratics already equal to zero by factorising and setting each bracket to zero, since a product vanishes only when a factor does. Foundation: monic x² + bx + c cases including the difference of two squares. Higher adds a > 1 via the harder factorising page; rearranging first is the Higher sibling. (A18)

subtopics.title: Quadratics with no constant term
subtopics.description: Solving x² = 5x by factorising, since dividing by x loses the root x = 0.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve quadratics without a constant term, e.g. x² = 5x and 3x² + 12x = 0, by taking out the factor x, insisting on both roots and naming the error of dividing through by x, which throws away x = 0. Full two-bracket factorising is the sibling page. Both tiers. (A18)

subtopics.title: Rearranging a quadratic before solving
subtopics.description: Collecting everything on one side equal to zero before factorising.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A18 braces on quadratics requiring rearrangement. Collect every term onto one side equal to zero before factorising, e.g. x² = x + 6, x(x + 1) = 12, (x + 1)(x − 2) = 4, explaining why a product equal to a non-zero number says nothing about its factors. (A18)

subtopics.title: Completing the square
subtopics.description: Writing x² + bx + c as a squared bracket plus a correction.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A18 braces. Write x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² plus a correction, checked by expanding back; include odd b giving fractional forms, and a > 1 by factoring a out of the x terms. Solving from this form is the sibling page; turning points belong to graphs. (A18, A11)

subtopics.title: Solving by completing the square
subtopics.description: Solving from completed square form by rooting both sides, plus and minus.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A18 braces. Solve from completed-square form by isolating the bracket and rooting both sides with plus and minus, giving exact surd answers like x = −3 ± √7 as well as rounded decimals. The completing itself is the sibling page; the formula is an alternative route. (A18)

subtopics.title: The quadratic formula
subtopics.description: Substituting a, b and c with their signs, and reading exact answers as surds.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A18 braces. Substitute a, b and c with signs intact, handling −b and b² for negative b, and give exact surd or rounded answers. The DfE formulae appendix lists the quadratic formula among those candidates must memorise. Discriminant classification of root counts is A level. (A18)

subtopics.title: Choosing how to solve a quadratic
subtopics.description: Factorising when the factors are visible, the formula when they are not.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page comparing the A18 methods: factorise when factors are visible, the formula when they are not or decimals are wanted, completing the square when that form or a turning point is demanded; read exact-versus-rounded cues in question wording. Each method is taught on its own sibling page. (A18)

subtopics.title: Simultaneous equations by elimination
subtopics.description: Adding or subtracting equations to remove one unknown, then substituting back.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve linear pairs whose coefficients already match, adding or subtracting to remove one unknown — same signs subtract, opposite signs add — then substituting back and checking in both equations. Scaling first, substitution, worded setups and the linear-quadratic pair each have their own sibling page. Both tiers. (A19)

subtopics.title: Scaling before eliminating
subtopics.description: Multiplying one or both equations so a pair of coefficients match.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve linear pairs where one or both equations must be multiplied first so a coefficient pair matches, e.g. 3x + 2y = 7 with 2x − y = 7; scale every term, negative coefficients and non-integer solutions included, then eliminate as on the sibling page. Both tiers. (A19)

subtopics.title: Simultaneous equations by substitution
subtopics.description: Replacing one unknown with an expression from the other equation.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve linear pairs by substituting an expression for one unknown taken from the equation where its coefficient is already 1, e.g. y = 2x + 1 into 3x + 2y = 16, expanding brackets carefully. This is the method the Higher linear-quadratic page depends on. Both tiers. (A19)

subtopics.title: Forming simultaneous equations from a problem
subtopics.description: Turning two facts about two unknowns into a pair of equations to solve.
subtopics.coverNote: Translate two facts about two unknowns — tickets and totals, sums and differences, mixed baskets of prices — into a pair of linear equations, solve by either method, and interpret both values in context with units. Pure technique lives on the elimination and substitution siblings. Both tiers. (A19, A21)

subtopics.title: A linear and a quadratic equation together
subtopics.description: Substituting the linear equation into the quadratic, pairing each x with its y.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A19 braces on linear/quadratic pairs. Substitute the linear equation into forms like y = x² + 3x or x² + y² = r², solve the quadratic, and pair each x with its own y, presenting answers as coordinate pairs. The circle-geometry reading of this lives on line-meets-circle. (A19)

subtopics.title: Reading a solution off a graph
subtopics.description: The solutions of f(x) = k, where the graph meets the line at height k.
subtopics.coverNote: Find approximate solutions of f(x) = k by drawing the horizontal line at height k and reading crossings, on linear and quadratic graphs; include f(x) = 0 as the x-axis case and stress answers are estimates limited by the grid. Crossing lines and parabola roots have their own sibling pages. Both tiers. (A17, A18)

subtopics.title: Simultaneous equations as crossing lines
subtopics.description: The crossing point as the one pair of values satisfying both equations.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve a linear pair graphically: draw both lines and read the crossing point as the single value pair satisfying both equations, checking by substitution; connect to the algebraic methods and note parallel lines give no solution. Reading accuracy limits apply. Both tiers. (A19)

subtopics.title: Approximate quadratic solutions from a graph
subtopics.description: Reading roots where the parabola crosses the axis, and why they are estimates.
subtopics.coverNote: Read approximate roots where a drawn parabola crosses the x-axis, and solutions of a quadratic equal to k using a horizontal line; explain why graphical answers are estimates, checked by substitution. Exact algebraic solving is the quadratic group; iteration for refining approximations is Higher. Both tiers. (A18)

subtopics.title: Solving a linear inequality
subtopics.description: Solving with the balance method while keeping the inequality sign, since the answer is a range, not a value.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve linear inequalities in one variable with positive coefficients, e.g. 3x + 2 < 11 and 5x − 1 ≥ 2x + 8, keeping the inequality sign through each balance step; present answers as ranges like x < 3. Negative-coefficient flips, number lines and integer lists are the sibling pages. Both tiers. (A22)

subtopics.title: When the inequality sign reverses
subtopics.description: Multiplying or dividing by a negative flips the sign, every time and not just sometimes.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover the sign flip when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative, e.g. solving 5 − 2x > 11, alongside the alternative of moving the unknown to keep its coefficient positive; stress the flip happens on every such step and never for adding or subtracting. Both tiers. (A22)

subtopics.title: Inequalities on a number line
subtopics.description: Drawing the solution with an open circle for a strict inequality and a filled one when equality is allowed.
subtopics.coverNote: Represent solution sets on a number line: open circle for strict, filled circle for inclusive, arrows for unbounded ranges, segments for between-values like −2 < x ≤ 3; also read a drawn diagram back into symbols. Set notation and shaded 2D regions are the Higher siblings. Both tiers. (A22)

subtopics.title: Integer solutions of an inequality
subtopics.description: Listing the whole numbers a solution range contains, checking whether each endpoint is in or out.
subtopics.coverNote: List the integers satisfying an inequality or double inequality, e.g. −3 < x ≤ 2, checking each endpoint's inclusion; include finding the smallest or largest integer satisfying a solved inequality and combining two conditions. The solving itself belongs to the sibling pages. Both tiers. (A22)

subtopics.title: Solving a double inequality
subtopics.description: Applying every step to all three parts of an inequality like 3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 9.
subtopics.coverNote: Solve double inequalities like 3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 9 by applying every step to all three parts at once, or by splitting into two inequalities and recombining; present the answer as a single range and, where asked, list its integers via the sibling page. Both tiers. (A22)

subtopics.title: Set notation for solution sets
subtopics.description: Writing a solution as {x : x > 2}, and combining two separate ranges with a union.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A22 braces. Write solution sets as {x : x > 2}, express a between-range in one statement, and record two disjoint ranges, as from a quadratic inequality, with the union symbol. Reading and writing the notation only — the solving happens on the sibling pages. (A22)

subtopics.title: Regions from inequalities in two variables
subtopics.description: Shading the region satisfying several inequalities at once, with dashed boundary lines for the strict ones.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A22 braces on inequalities in two variables. Shade the region satisfying several inequalities at once, e.g. y > x, x + y < 6, x ≥ 1, with dashed boundaries for strict and solid for inclusive; identify integer points inside and describe a given region with inequalities. (A22)

subtopics.title: Solving a quadratic inequality
subtopics.description: Sketching the parabola to choose between the inside and the outside of the roots, rather than solving like an equation.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A22 braces. Solve quadratic inequalities in one variable by finding the roots and sketching the parabola to choose inside or outside, e.g. x² − x − 6 < 0; give answers as one range or two, in set notation where asked. Never solved like an equation. (A22)

subtopics.title: Forming an equation from words
subtopics.description: Naming the unknown, turning the facts into an equation, and checking the answer back in the story.
subtopics.coverNote: Name the unknown, translate the facts into a linear equation, solve it and check the answer against the story, in age, money and think-of-a-number contexts; answer the actual question asked, not just x. Geometric setups and quadratic outcomes are the sibling pages. Both tiers. (A21)

subtopics.title: Equations from angles and perimeters
subtopics.description: Using angle sums, perimeters and areas to set up an equation, then answering the geometric question asked.
subtopics.coverNote: Set up equations from angle sums in triangles and on straight lines, equal sides of named shapes, and perimeters and areas with algebraic lengths; solve, then give the angle or length asked for, not the x. The angle facts and mensuration formulae themselves live on the Geometry strand. Both tiers. (A21)

subtopics.title: Problems that lead to a quadratic
subtopics.description: Area and consecutive-number problems that produce a quadratic, where one root usually fails the context.
subtopics.coverNote: Form and solve quadratics from area, perimeter-with-area, consecutive-number and right-triangle problems, rejecting the root that fails the context, negative lengths especially. Foundation meets factorisable monic cases; setups needing the formula sit naturally at Higher. Solving technique lives on the quadratic group. (A18, A21)

subtopics.title: Showing a root lies in an interval
subtopics.description: Substituting both ends of the interval and citing the sign change between the two results.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page supporting A20 iteration. Show a root of f(x) = 0 lies between a and b by evaluating f at both ends and citing the sign change, with the caveat that the function is continuous; include trapping a root to one decimal place by further evaluations. (A20)

subtopics.title: Rearranging into iterative form
subtopics.description: Showing an equation can be rewritten as x = g(x), the shape an iteration formula needs.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A20 braces. Show that a given equation can be rearranged into a stated form x = g(x), typically by isolating an x term then rooting or dividing, working the algebra in both directions where asked. Choosing between rearrangements and convergence behaviour are A level concerns. (A20)

subtopics.title: Using an iteration formula
subtopics.description: Feeding each answer back into the formula from a starting value, and knowing when to stop.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A20 braces. Run xₙ₊₁ = g(xₙ) from a given starting value using the calculator ANS key, recording each iterate to sufficient decimals and stopping when successive values agree to the accuracy asked, then stating the root to that accuracy. Why iteration converges is A level. (A20)

topics.title: Sequences
topics.cardDescription: Term-to-term rules, special sequences, nth terms and Higher-tier quadratics.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE sequences: term-to-term rules, the special sequences worth recognising, and the nth term of linear and quadratic sequences.

subtopics.title: Term-to-term rules
subtopics.description: Continuing a sequence by the rule that moves one term to the next, stated with a starting term.
subtopics.coverNote: Continue sequences from a term-to-term rule with its starting term — add or subtract a constant, multiply by a constant, mixed rules like double then add 1 — and state the rule from given terms. Position-to-term rules and subscript notation are the sibling pages. Both tiers. (A23)

subtopics.title: Position-to-term rules
subtopics.description: Generating any term straight from its position, without stepping through every term before it.
subtopics.coverNote: Generate any term directly from a position-to-term rule given in words or as an expression like 3n + 1, without stepping through earlier terms, and compare the efficiency against term-to-term for distant terms. Finding the nth term yourself belongs to the linear nth term group. Both tiers. (A23)

subtopics.title: Recurrence relations
subtopics.description: Reading rules written as xₙ₊₁ = 2xₙ + 1, and building terms that may depend on the two before.
subtopics.coverNote: Read and use subscript notation: generate terms from rules like xₙ₊₁ = 2xₙ + 1 given x₁, including rules using the two previous terms, and work backwards to earlier terms. Both tiers. The same notation returns in the Higher iteration group on the equations topic. (A23)

subtopics.title: Sequences from growing patterns
subtopics.description: Counting matchsticks or tiles in each stage of a pattern, and predicting the next stage from the growth.
subtopics.coverNote: Count matchsticks, tiles or dots across the stages of a growing pattern, tabulate against stage number, predict later stages, and describe the growth in words. Turning the pattern into an nth term formula belongs to the linear nth term group. Both tiers. (A23, A25)

subtopics.title: Square and cube number sequences
subtopics.description: Recognising 1, 4, 9, 16 and 1, 8, 27, 64, and continuing them from position rather than difference.
subtopics.coverNote: Recognise and continue 1, 4, 9, 16 and 1, 8, 27, 64 from position, as n² and n³, rather than from differences; spot shifted versions like n² + 1 and find a stated term directly. General quadratic sequences are the Higher group. Both tiers. (A24)

subtopics.title: Triangular numbers
subtopics.description: The sequence 1, 3, 6, 10 built by adding one more each time, and the dot triangles behind it.
subtopics.coverNote: Recognise and continue 1, 3, 6, 10 from the add-one-more rule and the dot-triangle picture; find several further terms and pick triangular numbers out of given values. The formula n(n + 1)/2 may be quoted, but deriving quadratic nth terms is the Higher group. Both tiers. (A24)

subtopics.title: Fibonacci-type sequences
subtopics.description: Each term as the sum of the two before it, continued forwards and worked backwards from later terms.
subtopics.coverNote: Recognise and extend Fibonacci-type sequences, each term the sum of the two before, from any pair of starting values; work backwards from later terms, and run a few terms from algebraic starts a and b. Solving for unknown starts from a given later term suits Higher-leaning practice. Both tiers. (A24)

subtopics.title: Geometric sequences
subtopics.description: Sequences that multiply by a fixed ratio each step, such as powers of 2 or of a half.
subtopics.coverNote: Recognise and continue geometric sequences multiplying by a fixed positive rational ratio, e.g. powers of 2, of 10 or of ½, per A24's rⁿ wording; find the ratio from consecutive terms and link to repeated percentage growth on the Ratio strand. Surd ratios are the Higher sibling. Both tiers. (A24)

subtopics.title: Naming the type of a sequence
subtopics.description: Deciding from a few terms whether a sequence is linear, quadratic, geometric or Fibonacci, by differences and ratios.
subtopics.coverNote: Classify a sequence from a few terms as linear, quadratic, geometric, Fibonacci-type, triangular, square or cube, using first differences, second differences and ratios as the tests; justify the choice and continue the sequence. Both tiers — A24 lists recognition of all these, quadratic included, outside the braces. Higher may also meet an unfamiliar rule to continue, the A24 catch-all: other sequences. (A24)

subtopics.title: Geometric sequences with a surd ratio
subtopics.description: Sequences whose ratio is a surd like √2, simplified term by term so the pattern stays visible.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page, per the A24 braces on surd ratios. Continue and complete geometric sequences with ratios like √2 or 2√3, simplifying each term so the pattern stays visible, and find the ratio from consecutive surd terms. Surd arithmetic itself is taught on the Number strand. (A24)

subtopics.title: The nth term of a linear sequence
